title: Columnstore Indexes & TempDB Optimization
exp: Modern data platform interviews cover Columnstore for analytical queries and TempDB bottleneck resolution.
pts: **Clustered Columnstore Indexes (CCI):** compressed columnar storage, segment elimination, batch mode execution for analytics.
**Non-clustered Columnstore Indexes (NCCI):** added onto transactional OLTP tables for real-time operational analytics (HTAP).
**TempDB Contention:** `PAGELATCH_UP` / `PAGELATCH_EX` on allocation maps (PFS/GAM/SGAM) under high concurrency.
**Table Variables vs Temp Tables (`#tbl`):** `#tbl` has statistics and supports indexes; table variables lack column statistics (estimated 1 row).
code:
CREATE CLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX CCI_FactSales ON FactSales;
-- Enables batch mode processing and 10x-50x compression ratio
pr: Measure compression ratio of Columnstore on a sample table
Compare Temp Table vs Table Variable execution plans

r: Deep mechanics of Columnstore Indexes & TempDB Optimization under concurrent execution.
Always design for idempotency, cancellation propagation, and thread safety.
Memory allocation spikes or CPU bound thread starvation.
Use profiling tools to measure actual baseline allocation before optimizing.
Balancing developer velocity with operational maintenance complexity.
Favor simple, well-tested modular architectures over premature complexity.

qa.q: When should you use Columnstore indexes instead of B-Tree indexes?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use Columnstore for data warehousing, analytical queries scanning millions of rows, and aggregations (SUM, AVG). Columnstore uses column-based compression and batch mode execution. Stick to B-Tree indexes for OLTP workloads doing point lookups and single-row updates.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Indexes store data in B-Tree structures. Clustered indexes dictate physical row storage on disk leaf pages; non-clustered indexes point to clustered keys or RIDs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Over-indexing degrades write performance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations and leads to index fragmentation and page splits.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Covering indexes eliminate costly Key Lookups for read-heavy workloads but increase storage footprint and write transaction overhead.

qa.q: Why can Table Variables cause terrible performance for large datasets compared to Temp Tables?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Table Variables do not maintain column statistics. The query optimizer assumes a table variable has 1 row regardless of actual size, frequently choosing nested loop joins instead of hash joins and under-allocating memory.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.
